8% of children younger than 12 years of age in the United States experi-
enced prolonged periods in which they had insufficient food. Data from 
2012 indicated that 10% of U.S. households with children were food- 
insecure. In 2012, 49.0 million people in the United States lived in food-
insecure households; 15.9 million of those people (11.3%) were children 
(Food and Research Action Center, 2014). A longitudinal study following 
approximately 21,000 children from kindergarten through third grade 
found that persistent food insecurity was predictive of impaired aca-
demic outcomes, poorer social skills, and a tendency to increased BMI 
(Ryu and Bartfeld, 2012).
Although these studies have limitations because of other factors that 
may affect a child’s functioning (e.g., stress, family dysfunction, or sub-
stance abuse), a correlation exists between children’s lack of sufficient 
food and their behavioral and academic functioning. As future studies 
provide more evidence of this relationship, it will be clear that social 
policies must ensure the provision of children’s basic needs for optimal 
growth and development.
